title: He loved them to the end (John 13:1–17)
word: He loved them to the end
hook: he washes the feet of every disciple, even Judas

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus's last public words in John, like a friend at sunset. Your line was while you have the light. What good thing did you do before dark? Day six hundred twenty-eight.

In Jesus's world, people walked everywhere in sandals, on dirt roads shared with donkeys and sheep. Arriving at a house for dinner, your feet were filthy. A good host had water ready, and usually the lowest servant in the house did the washing. It was a job nobody wanted. Now the evening before Passover. Jesus and his friends are at supper. Nobody has washed anyone's feet. And John opens the second half of his Gospel with one of the most tender sentences he ever wrote.

"Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Unto the end can mean two things in Greek. To the last moment, and also to the uttermost, completely. Both are true here. Then Jesus gets up from supper, takes off his outer robe, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant. "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded." Picture the room going silent. When he gets to Peter, Peter refuses: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." It's wrong, it's upside down. Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter swings to the opposite extreme: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." Peter is always all or nothing. Here's the detail that stops the heart. John has just told us that the devil had already put it into Judas's heart to betray him. And Jesus knows. He says so: not all of you are clean. And he washes every disciple's feet anyway. Including the feet that will walk out of this room to betray him. When he's done, he puts his robe back on and says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Churches keep this command differently. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and others wash feet in the Holy Thursday service. Some churches, like many Mennonites and Brethren, wash feet regularly as an ordinance. Others hear it mainly as a call to humble service.
screen: `TO THE LAST, AND TO THE UTTERMOST.`
then, large: `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve someone you find difficult. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's hard for you. Not dangerous, just difficult. A coworker who grates on you, a relative you avoid, someone who let you down. Picture them clearly. Now picture yourself doing one small, humble thing for them. Making their coffee. Helping with a task. Saying something kind about them to someone else. Notice the resistance in you. Let it be there. If you pray, you can ask for the humility to serve them anyway. If you don't, simply hold the picture for a moment. The bell holds the time.
He loved them to the end. John's opening to the Last Supper: Jesus loved his own to the last and to the uttermost, and washed their feet.

segments.voice: Your line: to the end. Today, do the one humble thing you pictured for the difficult person, and don't mention it. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Many churches wash feet on Holy Thursday, the evening before Good Friday; some, including many Mennonite and Brethren churches, practice footwashing regularly, and others keep the command through acts of humble service.

original.note: Greek: to the end, to completion. It can mean to the last moment, or to the uttermost.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice gesture of humility.
what it means: the night before he dies, Jesus takes the lowest servant's job and washes every disciple's feet, including Judas's.
what a scholar hears: eis telos means both to the end and to the uttermost, and chapter thirteen opens what many call John's Book of Glory.

notes: Footwashing practices: Holy Thursday (Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, others); ordinance in many Mennonite, Brethren, some Baptist and Adventist churches. Confirm.
'Usually the lowest servant': footwashing by slaves; confirm generalization (cf. 1 Samuel 25:41).
The text implies Judas's feet were washed (13:2, 10–11) without stating it outright; confirm phrasing.
KJV 'bason' is the 1769 spelling; inside quotation.
